chapters.title: Five Pillars of Good Writing
blocks: What qualities good writing should have · How IELTS Writing is marked

Before taking IELTS, almost everyone has one question in mind: "My English is fairly good, so why do I have so much trouble with IELTS writing?" The answer is very simple. IELTS is not actually a different kind of writing - it is ordinary good English writing with a specific format placed on top of it. In other words, there are two jobs:
First, learn to write correct, clear English.
Then, learn the specific mould (format) of Task 1 and Task 2.

This chapter is about the first job. The funny thing is, we have taken English exams all our lives and memorised essays, but nobody ever told us clearly "what good writing must contain". As a result, even many university graduates cannot answer this question. The points below will help you not only in IELTS but everywhere - job emails, reports, applications.
Good writing has five qualities. Let us look at them one by one.
1. Correctness - writing must be free of mistakes

Small slips, such as teh / recieve, are called "slips of the pen". If there are not too many, they do little harm. But a spelling mistake that changes the meaning of the word is treated by the examiner as "using the wrong word" - this is far more serious:
advice = a suggestion (noun); advise = to give a suggestion (verb)
lose = to misplace / fail to keep; loose = not tight
then = after that; than = used in comparisons
affect = to have an influence on (verb); effect = influence / result (noun)
test = an exam / check; taste = flavour
Make a list of the 10 words you yourself misspell again and again. In the last 2–3 minutes of the exam, look for just those.
All grammatical mistakes are bad, but there are five types of mistake that immediately tell the examiner the writer's foundation is weak. These are all grammar from the lower classes of school:
Yesterday I go to the market.
Yesterday I went to the market.
The number of cars have increased.
The number of cars has increased.
Teachers and parents think they are lazy. (Who is lazy?)
Teachers and parents think students are lazy.
Fix these five before thinking about "advanced" grammar. A student who writes 15 simple but correct sentences will get a higher band than one who writes 10 complex sentences with 6 mistakes.
2. Vocabulary / Lexical resource - range of words
Whether your writing is good can be seen from the words you use. The examiner looks at your range of vocabulary - how many different words you can use correctly. Two rules:
Rule A: accurate, slightly uncommon words instead of common ones - if you are sure
Most students recycle the same 200 common words in every essay. If you can put a more precise word in place of a common one, and you are sure it is correct, then use it:
Students remember essays and write them in the exam. → Students memorise essays and reproduce them in the exam.
a big problem → a serious / major / significant problem
But be careful: using an uncommon word wrongly loses more marks than using a common word correctly. Do not use a word in the exam that you have never seen inside a sentence.
Rule B: not the same word again and again - use synonyms
Suppose the question is: Why do you want to study in a foreign country? Someone wrote:

I want to study in a foreign country because foreign universities are better than universities in my country. Foreign universities have better teachers. If I study in a foreign country I can get a part-time job.
The writing is not wrong, but "foreign" appears four times and "universities" three times - it feels monotonous to read, and the examiner assumes the writer's vocabulary is small. Now the same idea:

I want to study abroad because overseas institutions offer higher standards than those at home. Their teachers are better qualified, and studying in another country would also allow me to work part-time.
The same meaning, but foreign → abroad → overseas → in another country; universities → institutions → those. This is the easiest way to raise your vocabulary score.

Before you start writing, look at the key nouns in the question and write two synonyms for each on the question paper. For example: children → young people, minors, the young; technology → digital tools, devices, innovation.
3. Sentence structure - how sentences are built
Many people think good writing means every sentence is long and complex. That is only half true. Good writing has a mix of three kinds of sentence:
Traffic is heavy in the morning.
Two ideas joined with and / but / so / or
Traffic is heavy in the morning, so many people leave early.
Main idea + a dependent part (because, although, which, when, if…)
Although the metro is fast, many people still drive because they dislike crowds.
Rough guide: one complex sentence after every two simple/compound sentences.

**Golden rule:** A correct simple sentence is always better than an incorrect complex sentence. If you are not sure, break the long sentence into two short sentences and join them with a linking word.
A very common mistake - the double connector. In English, only one joining word goes between two clauses:
✗ Although it was raining, but we went out.   ✓ Although it was raining, we went out. / It was raining, but we went out.
✗ Because he was late, so he missed the bus.   ✓ Because he was late, he missed the bus.
✗ Despite of the rain…   ✓ Despite the rain… / In spite of the rain…
4. Using correct form of voice - Active or Passive?
Among students in our country there is a belief that writing in the passive voice makes writing sound "weighty" or "academic". This is a misconception. Compare:
The decision has been supported by my friends. (passive - heavy, roundabout)
My friends have supported the decision. (active - direct, clear)
The new method is believed to be effective by the teachers. (passive)
The teachers believe that the new method is effective. (active - better)
The active voice is the natural choice. It makes writing lively and strong. Use the passive only in the five cases below:
Who did it (the doer) is not important; the action is what matters
Rice is grown across the delta.
My bicycle was stolen last night.
You deliberately want to keep the doer's name hidden
Several complaints have been made about the service.
Describing a process / method (this is exactly what a Task 1 flow chart needs)
The beans are roasted, then ground, and finally packed.
A polite suggestion to someone senior
This report should be checked again before Friday.
Apart from these five, write in the active voice everywhere else.
Coherence is the biggest topic of this chapter, and it is directly one of the IELTS marking criteria (Coherence & Cohesion). To understand it, you first need to understand what a paragraph is.
A paragraph is a group of sentences that discusses one specific idea. An essay is divided into paragraphs so that the reader can see each idea separately and follow it easily.
How long should a paragraph be?
There is no strict rule, but long paragraphs tire the reader. In modern writing, 80–150 words (roughly 5–8 lines) is ideal.
Beyond 200 words, the reader loses the thread.
For special emphasis you can write a one-sentence paragraph (10–15 words) - this is called an emphatic paragraph. Use it very rarely, and never in Task 1.
Two things are needed to be coherent
Relevance: every sentence stays within the same idea.
Order / Organization (the right sequence): the sentences are arranged in a logical flow.
A good paragraph starts with a topic sentence - in one sentence it tells you what the paragraph is about. Every other sentence should support this topic sentence. Read the paragraph below:

City life and village life are very different. In the city, people work long hours in offices. Long hours make people tired. Tired people often argue with their family. Family arguments can lead to divorce. Divorce is increasing in my country.

The first sentence (the topic sentence) says the paragraph will be about the differences between city and village life. But from the second sentence the writing moves to work → tiredness → family quarrels → divorce. Each sentence is connected to the one before it, but the paragraph as a whole has moved away from the topic sentence (drift). This is a failure of relevance - very common, and a very costly mistake in IELTS.
How to check it yourself: cover everything except the topic sentence. Then read each sentence one by one and ask - "Does this support the topic sentence?" If it does not, cut it or move it.

Another trap - a vague topic sentence. "Many people move to cities." - is the paragraph about why they go, what problems arise, or what the benefits are? The reader cannot tell. Make the topic sentence specific: "People move to cities for three main reasons."
Even if every sentence is relevant, a paragraph is not coherent if the order is jumbled. Here is the same paragraph above, rewritten to be relevant and ordered:

City life and village life differ in three important ways. First, work in the city is mostly in offices and factories with fixed hours, whereas village work follows the seasons. Second, city families are usually small and live far from relatives, but village families are large and neighbours are often cousins. Finally, the cost of living is much higher in the city, especially rent, while villagers often own their land and grow their own food.

Notice the pattern: topic sentence → point 1 (city, then village) → point 2 (city, village) → point 3 (city, village). Every sentence supports the topic sentence, and the reader always knows where they are.

chapters.title: Cohesion - connective / signpost words
blocks: The paragraph above uses First, Second, Finally, whereas, but, while. These are called connective words, transition signals or signpost words. They tell the reader in advance what kind of sentence comes next: a new point? The opposite view? An example? A result?

Without connectives, writing reads like a list of separate sentences. With connectives, the ideas flow. IELTS gives marks for this directly. Connectives have nine jobs. We will build a paragraph - about "living in a big city" - and show each job.
1. Starting information - beginning the first point
To begin with, a large city offers far more jobs than a small town.
More: First of all, Firstly, In the first place.
2. Adding similar information - adding the same kind of information
In addition, the best schools and hospitals are usually in the city.
More: Moreover, Furthermore, Besides, Also, Similarly, Likewise, What is more.
For instance, all the country's top universities are in the capital.
More: For example, Such as, To illustrate, In particular, Namely, A case in point is.
However, city life also brings serious problems.
More: In contrast, On the other hand, Nevertheless, Whereas, While, Although, Yet, Conversely, Despite this.

⚠️ **On the contrary** does not mean "on the other hand". It means "rather, the opposite is true". It is used only to reject a mistaken idea: He is not lazy; on the contrary, he works twelve hours a day.
In short, the problems of city living cannot be ignored.
More: In brief, Briefly, To put it simply, Overall.
Clearly, Undoubtedly, Certainly, Without doubt, Obviously, Of course
It seems that, Arguably, Apparently, To some extent, It is true that, Fortunately / Unfortunately
Undoubtedly, anyone moving to the capital must accept a lower quality of air.
⚠️ Never write "According to me". Write: In my view / In my opinion / I believe.
Consequently, thousands of people migrate to the capital every year.
More: As a result, Therefore, Thus, Hence, For this reason, As a consequence, This leads to.
At present I am an undergraduate. At the same time, I am learning to code. After that, I plan to do a master's degree.
At present, Currently, Nowadays, At this time
After that, Subsequently, Afterwards, Eventually, Later
In conclusion, city life offers opportunity at a price.
More: To sum up, To conclude, In summary, Overall.
⚠️ Do not use "At last" (it means "finally, after a long wait"). Do not start a conclusion with "Last but not least".
See the difference - the same paragraph twice

Online learning has grown fast. Students can study from anywhere. They can watch a lesson many times. It is cheaper than a classroom course. There are problems. Students feel alone. Many stop before the end. Online learning is useful. It cannot replace a good teacher.

Online learning has grown fast in recent years. To begin with, students can study from anywhere, and moreover they can watch a lesson as many times as they like. In addition, it is far cheaper than a classroom course. However, there are problems. Many students feel isolated, and as a result a large number give up before the end. In short, online learning is useful, but it cannot yet replace a good teacher.
The same sentences, the same ideas - but the second one feels like "writing", while the first is a shopping list.
Overuse: if every sentence starts with a connective, the writing sounds mechanical - the examiner writes "over-use" and you get stuck at band 6. Aim: one every two or three sentences.
Wrong logic: Moreover before an opposing point, or As a result before something that is not a result - the examiner concludes you do not understand the word's meaning.
Punctuation: a connective at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma (However, …). Whereas / while / although join two clauses in the middle of one sentence, with no capital letter in between.
in addition, moreover, furthermore, besides, also, similarly, likewise, as well as, not only … but also, then, too

as a result, consequently, therefore, thus, hence, so, for this reason, it follows that, this leads to, eventually, in that case

however, nevertheless, nonetheless, in contrast, on the other hand, whereas, while, although, even though, though, despite / in spite of (+noun), yet, but, conversely, instead of, rather, compared with, on the contrary (with care)

**Remember:** Using connective words is extremely important not only for IELTS but for any English writing. Pick 2–3 words from each row and keep using them until they feel natural.

chapters.title: Your writing through the examiner's eyes: marking and bands
blocks: Of the four IELTS modules, two (Reading and Listening) are objective - each question has only one correct answer, and you can work out your band yourself by checking the answer sheet. But Writing and Speaking are subjective - a trained examiner assesses them, and the same piece of writing may get a slightly different band from two examiners.

This creates a problem: if you prepare alone, you cannot see your own mistakes, and you do not know your real band either. In this chapter the examiner's checklist is given in simple language - so that you at least know what they look for. (Even so, you still need feedback from a teacher or the app's AI grader.)

Every Task 1 and Task 2 answer is scored on four separate criteria, each weighted 25%. Their average is the band for that task. Remember: in the final Writing band, Task 2 carries twice the weight of Task 1.
Did you do exactly what the question asked?
Is it organised in clear paragraphs with good linking?
Is the vocabulary wide and accurate, with correct spelling?
A variety of sentence types, mostly error-free?
2, 3 and 4 are the same in both tasks - they were discussed in the first part of this chapter. Only number 1 is different:
Task Achievement (Task 1): report the main features of the visual, give an overview, accurate data, comparisons, 150+ words, no opinion.
Task Response (Task 2): answer every part of the question, a clear position, ideas developed with reasons and examples, 250+ words.
You did part of the task, not all of it; the format was also wrong in places.
There is no clear overview, or if there is one it is very general - not supported with data.
You mentioned some key points, but not enough; instead you wrote more about less important data.
You answered the question only partly; the format was not always right.
You have a position, but it is not always clear; there is no proper conclusion.
There are some ideas, but they are not developed; some parts are irrelevant.
Information is roughly organised, but progression is limited.
You used connectives, but too few, wrongly, or far too many.
For lack of ideas, you repeated the same thing again and again.
Paragraphs were not divided properly, or you did not use paragraphs.
Vocabulary is limited; it gets the job done, but it is not enough.
Frequent spelling mistakes and wrong words; sometimes hard to read.
Mostly simple sentences; attempts at complex sentences are usually wrong.
Many grammar and punctuation mistakes; in places the meaning is hard to understand.
You attempted everything the task asked you to write.
There is an overview, and the information is selected appropriately.
You caught the key points, but the details contain some errors or irrelevant information.
You answered all parts of the question, though some parts better than others.
The position is clear, although the conclusion is unclear.
The main ideas are there, but some are not properly developed.
Information is arranged logically, with clear progression.
You used connectives well, but sometimes mechanically or wrongly.
You used paragraphs, but not always logically.
You used adequate vocabulary; there are attempts at less common words, with some errors.
There are spelling / word errors, but they do not get in the way of understanding.
You used both simple and complex sentences.
There are some grammar and punctuation mistakes, but the meaning is clear.
You did everything that was required.
You clearly showed the main trends and differences.
You covered the key points properly; they could have been developed further.
You answered all parts of the question properly.
A clear position throughout the writing.
Main ideas are well presented and explained; supporting ideas lose focus in places.
All information and ideas are logically organised and progress smoothly.
You used connectives in a range of situations; under/over-use in one or two places.
Paragraphs are good, each with a clear central topic.
A wide range of words, used accurately; less common words used well.
A variety of complex sentences, with correct structure and use.
Very few grammar and punctuation mistakes.
You wrote everything the task required, appropriately.
You presented and explained all the key points well.
All aspects of the task are well covered.
You used relevant, detailed supporting ideas.
All information and ideas are logically arranged.
Paragraphing is sufficient and appropriate; the linking is barely noticeable.
A varied vocabulary, used fluently and accurately.
Uncommon words used skilfully; errors are rare.
A range of sentence structures used skilfully.
Everything in Band 8, with only the rare slip that even an educated native writer makes under time pressure. Completely natural, flawless, and every demand of the task fulfilled.
Read the ladder - where the big jumps are
From "partial" to "all parts"; an overview appears; the position becomes clear
Answer every part of the question; always write an overview in Task 1; state your opinion in the introduction itself in Task 2
From "some errors" to "very few errors"; ideas get developed; linking becomes natural
Cut any sentence you are not sure of; give explanation + example for every idea; fewer but accurate connectives
From "good" to "skilled and precise"; almost no errors
More precise, wider vocabulary; more variety in structure; one full revision pass

**The most common reason for getting stuck at Band 6:** the writing is mostly correct, but the ideas are only listed, not developed; and every paragraph has one or two "clumsy" mistakes. Both can be fixed.
Estimate your own band - a quick self-test
After writing an answer, tick honestly:
I answered every part of the question (T2) / I reported the main features with an overview (T1).
My position is clear in the introduction and conclusion (T2 only).
Every idea has at least one sentence of explanation, and in Task 2 an example.
Only one topic in each paragraph.
One linking word every two or three sentences - not in every sentence.
No linking word is repeated, and none is used with the wrong meaning.
No key noun appears more than twice in one paragraph.
I did not use any word I am unsure of.
I checked my usual spelling mistakes.
At least one correct complex sentence in each paragraph.
I checked subject–verb agreement and tense.
All ticked → probably Band 7 or above. Half ticked → Band 6. Fewer → Band 5. Do this after every practice, before looking at the AI feedback.

chapters.title: Task 1 ground rules
blocks: Word limit - how many words to write
The rule is a minimum of 150 words. But no upper limit is given, so everyone asks: what is the maximum? The answer in one word - 180.
Never fewer than 150. Even if you write 148 words, you lose marks.
Don't go above 200. The more words, the more chances of mistakes, and the less time for Task 2 (which carries double the weight).
The space on the answer sheet easily fits an answer of 170–180 words. If you need an extra sheet, you'll know you are writing too much.
What counts as a word and what doesn't
IELTS's official rule is simple: everything you write is a word - a, an, the, in, of, numbers (2010), percentages - everything. A hyphenated word is one word (twenty-five = 1 word).
But keep two things in mind:

Sentences copied word for word from the question are not "your writing" in the examiner's eyes. Even if those words are counted, they are not taken as evidence of your ability; on the contrary, they give the impression that you "can't paraphrase".

Examiners don't sit and count words - they don't have that much time. They estimate the length by eye. So don't waste time counting in the exam hall; instead, find out beforehand how many lines 170 words take up in your handwriting (usually 12–14 lines).
Any piece of writing has three parts: introduction, body, conclusion. In Task 1 we will write four paragraphs:
What the visual shows - in your own words
The 2–3 biggest features, without any numbers
Details of the first group, with numbers
Details of the second group, with numbers and comparisons

**Why is the overview the second paragraph?** Many books tell you to write the overview at the end as a "conclusion". That works too, but there is a risk: if you run out of time, the overview is what gets left out, and without an overview a whole band is lost in Task Achievement. So write the overview right after the introduction. If you have time, you can add a one-line closing sentence at the end - no harm if you don't.
The body can also have three paragraphs if the data naturally falls into three parts; but two is the safe default.

The IELTS authority says 20 minutes for Task 1. The reason: in Task 1 all the data is given, so once you learn the method, writing it is comparatively easy. Task 2 carries much more importance and weight.
Read the visual, understand the axis/unit/legend, mark the main points

We say it firmly: never take more than 20 minutes on Task 1 under any circumstances. Many people write Task 1 very carefully and at length, then rush to finish Task 2 - that's a bad bargain. When 20 minutes are up, finish the sentence you are on and move to Task 2.
In IELTS, roughly 7 types of Task 1 appear:

Most of the time a single type appears on its own. Sometimes a combination of two types appears (e.g. bar chart + pie chart). How to write each type is shown in detail with graphs in the following parts; so for now just remember the names.

Task 1 assesses whether you can describe the given data well. So any opinion, any explanation of "why this happened", any advice - is completely forbidden. "I think / I believe / probably because of the pandemic" - even one sentence like this lowers Task Achievement, because that information is not in the chart.
The report is impersonal. Write The chart shows…, never We can see… or You can notice….
3. Never start writing without fully understanding the graph (V.V.I)

Read everything - the title, the labels of both axes, the unit, the legend. Ask yourself: what is being measured? In which unit? Over what period? How many categories? Start writing only when you can explain it to yourself in one sentence. If you start writing before understanding it, you end up describing the wrong thing.
The first sentence (The graph shows…) is always in the present tense.
If the visual has past years, describe the data in the past tense: Sales rose in 2010.
If there is no year, use the present: Most households recycle glass.
If there are future years, not will/shall - write: is expected / projected / forecast / predicted / anticipated to + verb: Solar output is expected to triple by 2030.
Process and diagram → present simple, usually passive: The pulp is then dried.

No, it's optional. If an overview is written, the conclusion only repeats it. If you have time write one line; if not, leave it out - it won't affect your score. If you write one, it is a summary; never an opinion.

**Task 1 - what to avoid (avoid-list)**
▸ No opinion / advice / explanation of causes.
▸ No I, we, you.
▸ No copying sentences from the question.
▸ Never write without an overview; no numbers in the overview.
▸ No writing out every number one by one ("data dump").
▸ Not the same trend verb or the same connective three times.
▸ In a combination task, don't compare one graph with another - comparison is always within the same graph. (If there are several pie charts, compare between the pies.)
▸ Not more than 200 words, not more than 20 minutes.
▸ No bullets, headings or notes - paragraphs in full sentences.

**Task 1 - what to make sure of (must-list)**
**For line, column/bar and pie charts:**
▸ If there is a chance to compare, always compare.
▸ Always use connective words.
▸ Use synonyms for the question's words as far as possible (shows → illustrates; number → figure; percentage → proportion).
▸ If no time is mentioned, present tense; if it is, the tense that matches that time.
▸ If there are several pie charts, inter-compare between the pies.
**For flow charts and diagrams:**
▸ Passive form in most cases.
▸ Cycle or non-cycle - pay attention. If it is a cycle, you can start the description from any point you like; if not a cycle, from the starting point.
▸ If the diagram has specific segmentation (divisions), paragraph according to those divisions.
▸ Above all: describe by following the arrows.
▸ A conclusion isn't needed; if no time is mentioned, present tense (flow charts usually don't have one).
Language of numbers and comparison - needed in every type
Preposition - the most common grammar mistake in Task 1
Wrong preposition = wrong data = lower Task Achievement. "increased to 20%" and "increased by 20%" mean completely different things.

chapters.title: Line Graph step by step: Introduction and Overview
blocks: The line graph comes up most often, and what you learn here (introduction, overview, the language of trends, comparison) is what you'll use in every other type. So read this part slowly and attentively.

You should spend about 20 minutes on this task.
The graph below shows the number of visitors (in thousands) to Greenhill National Park between 1990 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
You should write at least 150 words.
I'll teach two methods of writing the introduction: (1) the Five-Question Method, (2) the Sentence-Frame Method. Learn both; in the exam, use whichever comes to mind faster.
Find the answers to five questions from the graph - you'll get all the ingredients of the introduction:
1. What type of graph is it?
visitors more than doubled overall, with a big drop in the mid-2010s
Just arrange the first four answers together and you have the first sentence:
The line graph shows the number of visitors to a national park, in thousands, from 1990 to 2020.
But this is almost a copy of the question. Now let's change the words:
illustrates, depicts, gives information about, presents, compares (if there are several lines)
how many people visited, visitor numbers, the figures for visitors, the amount of visitors (✗ - people are countable, so number/how many)
"in + unit" structure: in thousands / in metric tonnes / in per cent / in US dollars
from 1990 to 2020 · over a thirty-year period ending in 2020 · over three decades from 1990 · for 30 years up to 2020 · in the period 1990–2020
Six structures for the duration - avoid the one in the question and take a different one:
For (period) up to ______ (For 30 years up to 2020)
From ______ for the next/following (period) (From 1990 for the next 30 years)
Over a period of ______ up to ______ (Over a period of 30 years up to 2020)
In ______ (when there is only a single year)
Now add answer number 5 as the second sentence. The full introduction:

The line graph illustrates how many people visited Greenhill National Park, in thousands, over the thirty years from 1990 to 2020. Visitor numbers more than doubled over the period despite a sharp fall in the mid-2010s.
In this method you fill in the blanks of a fixed format with information from the question:

**Sentence 1:** The [line / bar / column graph · pie chart · table · diagram] + [describes / exhibits / illustrates / compares / demonstrates / indicates] + [information - paraphrased] + [measurement - in + unit] + [duration]
**Sentence 2:** Gist - highest / lowest / biggest rise / biggest fall - any one of them.
Three more kinds of introduction for the same graph - notice that the words and order are different in each, and the gist is different too:
The line graph describes the number of people who visited Greenhill National Park, in thousands, between 1990 and 2020. The lowest figures were recorded in the first five years.
The given line graph demonstrates the annual visitor figures for Greenhill National Park, measured in thousands, from 1990 for the following three decades. Attendance peaked in 2020.
Visitor numbers at Greenhill National Park have been depicted through the line graph in thousands over a period of 30 years up to 2020. The steepest decline occurred between 2010 and 2015.
An introduction written in a slightly uncommon format helps you get a higher score. But be careful - the first sentence of the introduction must be in the present tense.
Overview = the 2–3 biggest points of the graph, without any numbers. What you can say:
When / which is highest and lowest
The position at the end compared with the start
Any major exception (a big slump, a crossover)
With several lines: who is at the top and who is at the bottom at the end
Words to start with: Overall, … / It is clear that … / The most striking feature is …
Overall, visitor numbers rose considerably over the period, although the growth was interrupted by a sharp decline in the mid-2010s. The figure at the end of the period was the highest recorded.

chapters.title: Line Graph: Body, trend language and Conclusion
blocks: In the body paragraphs we will describe the main information of the graph. How much you write will depend on how much information the graph has:
If the graph has a lot of information, write only the main / significant data and trends.
If the graph has little information, you have to describe almost all of it - because under 150 words means negative marking.
comparison of start and end; two equal values

As soon as you get the question, mark all the significant points and trends on the graph (you can mark the IELTS question paper as you like). Give a number to every trend you have marked - then you'll know how many things you need to discuss:
5 trends are marked in the picture

To explain each change you need a verb (direction: did it rise or fall). Changes differ in type / size, so the verb needs an adverb (how strongly / how much). You also need to say over what period and by how much it changed. In other words, a trend description has five things:

**Subject + verb + adverb + time + amount changed**
Visitor numbers + rose + sharply + between 1995 and 2005 + to 480,000.
remained stable / steady / constant / unchanged, stayed at, levelled off, plateaued, maintained the same level, showed no change
stability, a plateau, a levelling-off, no change
rose, increased, grew, climbed, went up, ascended
a rise, an increase, growth, a climb
soared, surged, jumped, rocketed, shot up, leapt, boomed
a surge, a jump, a boom, a leap
fell, declined, decreased, dropped, dipped, went down, reduced
a fall, a decline, a decrease, a drop, a dip
plunged, plummeted, slumped, collapsed, dived, halved
a plunge, a slump, a collapse
peaked at, reached a high / low of, hit a low of, bottomed out at
a peak, a high, a low, a trough
Adverbs / adjectives by size of change
dramatically, sharply, steeply, considerably, significantly, substantially, markedly, drastically, rapidly, quickly
dramatic, sharp, steep, considerable, significant, substantial, marked, drastic, rapid
slightly, marginally, a little, minimally, slowly
Trend 1 needs no adverb, because there is no change. For the rest, choose the right adverb, and for similar changes don't repeat the same adverb - take a different one.
Now sentences for each trend - in three formats
Each trend can be written in three ways: (a) verb + adverb, (b) There was a + adjective + noun, (c) a single strong verb (no adverb). In the exam, mix all three so that the structure doesn't repeat.
(a) The number of visitors remained constant / stable / unchanged at 200,000 between 1990 and 1995.
(b) There was no change in visitor numbers for the first five years, which stayed at 200,000.
(c) Visitor numbers plateaued at 200,000 from 1990 to 1995.
(a) Visitor numbers rose sharply / increased dramatically / grew rapidly by 280,000 to 480,000 between 1995 and 2005.
(b) There was a dramatic / sharp / steep rise of 280,000 in the following decade, to 480,000.
(c) Attendance soared / surged / jumped to 480,000 in 2005, more than double the 1995 figure.
(a) The figure then fell slightly / dipped marginally by 10,000 to 470,000 in 2010.
(b) There was a slight / marginal / small dip in numbers over the next five years, to 470,000.
(a) Visitors fell sharply / dropped steeply / declined considerably by 120,000 to 350,000 between 2010 and 2015.
(b) There was a sharp / steep / considerable fall of 120,000 in the next five years, to 350,000.
(c) Attendance plunged / slumped / plummeted to 350,000 in 2015.
(a) The number climbed strongly / rose markedly by 170,000 to a peak of 520,000 in the last five years.
(b) There was a strong / marked recovery in the final period, with numbers reaching a high of 520,000.
(c) Visitors rebounded / recovered to a record 520,000 in 2020.
Extra: fluctuation - not in this graph, but it comes up in the exam
(a) The figure fluctuated considerably / varied widely between 300,000 and 430,000 over the period.
(b) There was considerable fluctuation in the figure, which moved between 300,000 and 430,000.
(c) Numbers oscillated between roughly 300,000 and 430,000 throughout.
Six ways to change the sentence order
To bring variety to the structure with the same information, you can move the elements around:
Information + verb + adverb + time + amount: Visitor numbers fell sharply between 2010 and 2015 by 120,000.
Information + verb + adverb + amount + time: Visitor numbers fell sharply by 120,000 between 2010 and 2015.
Time + information + verb + adverb + amount: Between 2010 and 2015, visitor numbers fell sharply by 120,000.
There was a + adjective + noun + in + information + time: There was a sharp fall of 120,000 in visitor numbers between 2010 and 2015.
Information + saw / experienced / recorded + a + adjective + noun + time: Visitor numbers saw a sharp fall between 2010 and 2015.
Time + saw + a + adjective + noun + in + information: The period 2010–2015 saw a sharp fall in visitor numbers.
Remember that repetition of structure and vocabulary will lower your score. And use connective words wherever applicable.

Let's split the five trends into two paragraphs: the first paragraph trends 1–2, the second paragraph trends 3–5. For each trend we pick one of the three formats above - so that the structure doesn't repeat:

For the first five years the number of visitors remained constant at 200,000. After 1995, however, the figure grew rapidly, reaching 480,000 in 2005, more than double the starting level.

This was followed by a decade of decline. Numbers dipped slightly to 470,000 in 2010 and then fell sharply to 350,000 over the next five years. In the final period the trend reversed, and visitors climbed to a peak of 520,000 in 2020, the highest figure recorded.
Notice: every sentence has a number, direction, degree and time; no structure appears twice; the connectives (however, this was followed by, then, in the final period) guide the reader.

A Task 1 conclusion is basically a summary of the whole task. It is optional - leave it out if you don't have time. If you do, take a concluding connective from the connective list and write one sentence: a notable point, or an overall summary.
In summary / To sum up / To recapitulate, despite the setback after 2010, the park attracted far more visitors at the end of the period than at the beginning.
Always remember: **no personal opinion may be written in a Task 1 conclusion.**

The line graph illustrates how many people visited Greenhill National Park, in thousands, over the thirty years from 1990 to 2020.

Overall, visitor numbers rose considerably over the period, although the growth was interrupted by a sharp decline in the mid-2010s. The figure at the end of the period was the highest recorded.

For the first five years the number of visitors remained constant at 200,000. After 1995, however, the figure grew rapidly, reaching 480,000 in 2005, more than double the starting level.

This was followed by a decade of decline. Numbers dipped slightly to 470,000 in 2010 and then fell sharply to 350,000 over the next five years. In the final period the trend reversed, and visitors climbed to a peak of 520,000 in 2020, the highest figure recorded.

In summary, despite the setback after 2010, the park attracted far more visitors at the end of the period than at the beginning.

This line graph is extremely simple - made to explain the basic concept. Real IELTS doesn't give such easy graphs; two or three lines, or a combination of a line graph with another graph, will come. Let's look at those now.

chapters.title: Graph with two lines - writing with comparison
blocks: The graph shows the percentage of households owning a car and a bicycle in one European city between 2000 and 2020.
Households owning a car / a bicycle, 2000–2020 (%)

Not only here - after receiving any Task 1, the first job is to understand the topic well. "Percentage of households owning a car and a bicycle" - means the graph shows what percentage of families have a car and what percentage have a bicycle, from 2000 to 2020. Two things to keep in mind: the data is about two different things (car and bicycle), and the data is from the past, so past tense.
Step 2 · Understanding the axes and details

The horizontal axis has years at 5-year intervals (2000, 2005 … 2020). The vertical axis has percentages, from 0 to 100. The two lines go in opposite directions - one is falling, one is rising - and in 2015 they cross each other (crossover). This crossing is the most important feature of the graph.
Car: rose slightly until 2005 (70 → 72), then fell for 15 years (72 → 48).
Bicycle: rose throughout the period (25 → 68), faster after 2005.
2020: bicycle 20 points above car - the exact reverse of the picture in 2000.
The graph has a lot of information and it's not possible to discuss it all (only 20 minutes in hand, and the word limit must be kept in mind too). So these four points are our report.
In the earlier structure: The ___ graph compares/describes + information + measurement + duration + main feature.

The line graph compares the proportion of households owning a car with the proportion owning a bicycle in a European city over two decades from 2000. Car ownership declined while bicycle ownership rose, and the two figures crossed in 2015.
Overall, cars became steadily less common and bicycles steadily more common, so that by the end of the period the bicycle had overtaken the car as the more widely owned of the two.
Many people write the two lines separately in two separate paragraphs, because this seems the easiest. But graph analysis means compare and contrast. Two ways to arrange the body:
By line: para 1 = car, para 2 = bicycle - each compared with the other.
By time: para 1 = 2000–2010, para 2 = 2010–2020 - both lines in each.
If the lines cross or change direction at the same time, "by time" is better, because then the crossover can be described directly. That's what we'll do here.
Start with the car trend, structure: information + verb + adverb + amount + time. Then the bicycle with a contrasting connective:

In 2000, cars were far more common than bicycles: 70% of households had a car, compared with only a quarter that had a bicycle. Car ownership edged up to 72% in 2005 before beginning to decline, falling to 65% by 2010. Meanwhile, bicycle ownership grew steadily, reaching 42% in the same year.

The following decade saw the gap close and then reverse. In 2015 both figures stood at exactly 55%. By 2020, however, car ownership had dropped to under half of households (48%), whereas the bicycle figure had climbed to 68%, twenty percentage points higher.
Language of comparison - what was used in this answer, and more
far more common than · compared with · only a quarter · meanwhile · in the same year · the gap closed · both stood at · whereas · twenty percentage points higher
twice as high as · the reverse was true for · the two lines converged / diverged · X overtook Y · the difference narrowed / widened · X lagged behind Y · X caught up with Y · at the same level as
⚠ **Percentage point:** from 25% to 40%, the increase is "15 percentage points", not "15 percent". (A 15 percent increase means 25 → 28.75.)

The line graph compares the proportion of households owning a car with the proportion owning a bicycle in a European city over two decades from 2000.

Overall, cars became steadily less common and bicycles steadily more common, so that by the end of the period the bicycle had overtaken the car as the more widely owned of the two.

In 2000, cars were far more common than bicycles: 70% of households had a car, compared with only a quarter that had a bicycle. Car ownership edged up to 72% in 2005 before beginning to decline, falling to 65% by 2010. Meanwhile, bicycle ownership grew steadily, reaching 42% in the same year.

The following decade saw the gap close and then reverse. In 2015 both figures stood at exactly 55%. By 2020, however, car ownership had dropped to under half of households (48%), whereas the bicycle figure had climbed to 68%, twenty percentage points higher.

In summary, the positions of the two vehicles were completely reversed over the twenty years.

chapters.title: Graph with many lines and future projections
blocks: To make the line graph completely clear, let's look at one more, slightly more complex graph.
The graph shows electricity generated from four sources in one country from 2000 to 2020, with projections to 2030 (terawatt-hours).

"Electricity generated from four sources … with projections" - the graph shows how much electricity was generated from four sources (coal, gas, wind, solar): actual data from 2000 to 2020, and an estimate for 2030. Compared with the earlier graphs this one is complex - but the method is the same.
Step 2 · Understanding the axes and details

Horizontal axis: 10-year intervals, 2000–2030. In the middle, at 2020, there is a dotted line - to its left is the past, to its right the future (the dotted lines are projections). Vertical axis: TWh, 0–120.
Some data is from the past, some from the future - be careful with tense. Past tense for the past. For the future, not will - specific vocabulary:

It is predicted / forecast / estimated / expected / projected / anticipated that X will …
X is expected / projected / forecast / predicted to + verb
The forecast / projection is for X to …
X is likely to …
Four lines - describing them all would go past 200 words. So select carefully, since there are so many trends involved:
Coal: largest at the start (120), then halved (60), projected to be almost zero (15) - the biggest fall.
Gas: rose and overtook coal (100), projected to fall slightly (80).
Wind: from almost zero to 45; projected to double and become the largest (90).
Solar: from zero to 25; projected to almost triple (70).
The main point: a shift from coal to renewables.
The line graph shows how much electricity was produced from coal, gas, wind and solar power in one country between 2000 and 2020, together with forecasts for 2030.

Overall, the country is moving away from coal towards renewable energy. Coal was the leading source at the start but is expected to be the smallest by 2030, while wind is projected to become the largest and gas peaks before declining.
Decide carefully in advance how you will divide the body paragraphs. Two options:
(i) Data for all fuels up to 2020 in para 1, projections in para 2.
(ii) Coal and gas (the large sources) in one para, wind and solar (renewables) in another.
Here we'll take (i), because splitting past/future keeps the tense clear too and makes compare/contrast easier.

In 2000 coal dominated, generating 120 TWh, twice the output of gas, while wind and solar produced almost nothing. Over the next twenty years coal fell by half to 60 TWh, and gas rose steadily to overtake it, reaching 100 TWh in 2020. Wind grew from 2 to 45 TWh in the same period, and solar, which had been zero, reached 25 TWh.

These trends are expected to continue and even accelerate. By 2030 coal is projected to fall to just 15 TWh, and gas is forecast to decline slightly to 80. In contrast, wind is predicted to double to 90 TWh, making it the largest source, and solar is expected to almost triple to 70 TWh.
Notice: para 1 has not a single projection word, while para 2 has one in every sentence (expected, projected, forecast, predicted) - and no word has been repeated.
Introduction paraphrased, one sentence, present tense.
Overview as the second paragraph, without numbers; the big trend + (with several lines) who is at the top/bottom at the end.
Select 4–6 key points (start, end, peak, trough, crossover, biggest change) - not every point.
Every trend sentence has direction + degree + number + time.
No verb, adverb or connective three times.
Preposition check: by / to / at / from…to.
Past data → past tense; projection → expected/projected language.

chapters.title: Part B - Bar / Column Graph
blocks: Everything you learned in Line graph - the four-paragraph template, the two methods of writing the introduction, the language of numbers - is exactly the same here. What changes is: how you find the story of the graph and how you arrange the body. Each type comes with one complete example, graph included.
Bar / Column Graph - step by step
First question: is there time or a category on the horizontal axis?
Like a line graph - trend, rises and falls
higher / lower than, the most, followed by
Both - compare the categories + how each one changed

⚠ The bars of categories do not "rise" or "fall". If there is no time and you write rose/fell, the examiner assumes you have not understood the graph. Write: X is higher than Y; X has the largest share.
The bar chart shows the amount of coffee consumed per person in five countries in 2022.
Unit: kg per person per year. Time: a single year (2022) - so not trend but comparison; tense: past (2022) or present - both work, but stick to one.
Highest: Finland (12); lowest: Japan (3.6). Finland is more than three times Japan.
Two groups can be seen: the two Nordic countries are far above (12, 9.9); the other three are below 6.
The bar chart compares how much coffee people in five countries drank per head in 2022, measured in kilograms per year.
Overall, the two Nordic countries consumed far more coffee than the other three, with Finland well ahead of every other nation and Japan at the bottom of the list.
In a category graph, arrange the body by group: para 1 = the top group, para 2 = the rest. In each group, state the order and the gaps.

Finland recorded the highest consumption by a clear margin, at 12 kg per person, followed by Norway with just under 10 kg. Between them, these two countries drank roughly twice as much coffee per head as any of the others.

The remaining three countries formed a distinct lower group. Brazil, despite being a major coffee producer, consumed 6.1 kg per person, about half the Finnish figure. The United States came next at 4.7 kg, while Japan had the lowest consumption of all, at 3.6 kg, less than a third of the amount in Finland.
(Here "despite being a major coffee producer" is general knowledge, not in the graph; even Band 7 writers sometimes slip this kind of thing in. If you want to stay safe, leave it out.)
The chart shows how people in the city of Riverton travelled to work in 2000 and 2020.
How people travelled to work in Riverton, 2000 and 2020
Unit: percentage (of commuters). Two years → past tense, and comparison in two directions: (a) between the modes in the same year, (b) between the two years for the same mode.
Car is the biggest in both years, but fell a lot (55 → 40). Bus also fell (25 → 20).
Train more than doubled (10 → 22), bicycle tripled (4 → 12). Walking unchanged (6).
The story: the city has moved away from the private car.
The bar chart compares the percentage of commuters in Riverton who used five different methods of transport to get to work in 2000 and in 2020.

Overall, the car remained the most popular way to travel to work in both years, but its share fell noticeably, while rail and cycling became far more common. Walking was the only mode that showed no change.
Step 6 · Body - "those that fell" and "those that rose"

In 2000, more than half of commuters (55%) drove to work, and a further quarter took the bus. By 2020 both of these figures had fallen, the car to 40% and the bus to 20%, although the car was still the leading choice.

In contrast, the share of people travelling by train or metro more than doubled, from 10% to 22%, making it the second most common mode in 2020. Cycling grew even faster in relative terms, tripling from 4% to 12%. Walking, meanwhile, stayed constant at 6% in both years.
the most / least popular · the largest / smallest share · the highest / lowest figure · in first / second place · followed by · at the bottom · the only category to …
accounted for · made up · represented · a quarter / a third / half of · one in five
more than doubled · tripled · halved · fell by … percentage points · in relative terms · by comparison · the reverse was true for
far higher than · slightly lower than · roughly the same as · twice as … as · X times more than · compared with · whereas · while

**Common mistakes in bar graphs:** (1) describing the bars one by one from left to right - instead, make groups: the big ones, the small ones, the ones that changed. (2) increased/decreased on a chart that has no time. (3) forgetting the unit (percentage? number? in thousands?).

chapters.title: Table - step by step
blocks: A table looks easy, but it is often the hardest type - because the trend is hidden inside the numbers and does not jump out at you the way it does in a graph. You have to find it yourself.
How to read a table (2 minutes)
Read the title, row labels, column labels and unit.
Look at each row from left to right: rising, falling, or the same?
Look at each column from top to bottom: which row is highest, which is lowest?
Mark: the biggest number, the smallest number, the total (if there is one), and any row/column that does not behave like the others.
Decide the groups: rows that behave in the same way go in the same paragraph.
The table shows the number of international students (in thousands) studying in four countries in 2010, 2015 and 2020.
Marked: red = highest, green = lowest, yellow = exceptions
Marked table: red = highest, green = lowest, yellow = exceptions
The USA is always the biggest, and it grew (690 → 1,075) - passing one million in 2020.
Australia is the only country where the number fell (330 → 290), then it rose strongly (460).
Canada was the smallest at the start (95), but grew more than five-fold (530) to almost equal the UK.
All of them are higher in 2020 than in 2010.
The table gives the number of overseas students, in thousands, enrolled in the USA, the UK, Australia and Canada at five-year intervals between 2010 and 2020.

Overall, all four countries hosted more international students at the end of the decade than at the start. The USA remained by far the largest destination throughout, while Canada, though the smallest in 2010, showed the fastest growth of all.
Para 1 = the two big, steadily growing countries (USA, UK). Para 2 = the two that broke the pattern (Australia, Canada).

The USA attracted 690,000 foreign students in 2010, already more than the other three countries combined. This figure climbed to 975,000 in 2015 and passed one million (1,075,000) by 2020. The UK, in second place, grew more slowly, from 400,000 to 430,000 and then to 550,000.

Australia was the only country whose numbers fell, dropping from 330,000 to 290,000 between 2010 and 2015, before recovering strongly to 460,000. Canada, meanwhile, recorded the most dramatic rise: its total of just 95,000 in 2010 nearly doubled to 170,000 by 2015 and then tripled again to 530,000, almost level with the UK.
Turn numbers into relationships: more than the other three combined · nearly doubled · almost level with · five times larger.
With a small table (4×3 = 12 numbers) you will need almost all the numbers; with a big table (6×5 = 30), 8–10 of them.
Mention whatever does not fit the pattern (the only country whose numbers fell) - an exception is always a "main feature".
Do not write in the order of the rows (top to bottom) - write in the order of behaviour.

chapters.title: Pie Chart - step by step
blocks: A pie chart shows parts of a whole. So the language here is not the language of trends but of proportion.
X accounts for / makes up / represents / constitutes 40% of the total · X takes up a quarter
the largest / smallest segment / share / proportion / category · the dominant use · a negligible 2%
half · just over / under half · a third · roughly a quarter · three-quarters · one in five · one in ten
the remaining 15% · the rest · together, A and B make up two-thirds · A and B combined
The pie chart shows the composition of household waste in one city.
Composition of household waste in one city
When there is only one pie: go from the biggest segment to the smallest, and group the small ones together. Overview = which segment(s) dominate. There is no time, so present tense.

The pie chart shows what proportion of the waste produced by households in one city falls into each of six categories.

Overall, food is by far the largest component, and food and paper together make up more than half of all household waste, whereas garden waste and miscellaneous items form only a small fraction.

Food waste accounts for just over a third of the total (34%), and paper and cardboard for a further 22%. These two categories combined therefore represent 56% of everything that households throw away. Plastics are the third largest category, at 18%, or almost one in five items.

The remaining three categories are considerably smaller. Glass and metal together make up 12%, garden waste 9%, and other materials just 5%, the smallest share on the chart. In total, these three account for roughly a quarter of household waste.
(160 words. Notice: there is not a single rose/fell; every number has a fraction or a comparison beside it.)
Two or more pie charts - what comes up more often in the exam

Usually the same thing in two years or in two places. Then the whole task is to compare the same segment across the two pies. Describing all of pie 1, then all of pie 2 - that is the classic Band 5 answer, because it contains no comparison.
The charts show how adults in one country spent their time online in 2015 and 2023.
How adults spent their time online
Entertainment (social media, video) rose a lot; use for information and work fell a lot.
The largest segment changed: in 2015 news (30%), in 2023 social media (40%).
The two pie charts compare the proportion of online time that adults in one country devoted to five activities in 2015 and 2023.

Overall, internet use shifted strongly from information and work towards entertainment. Social media replaced news as the largest single activity, and together with video streaming it came to account for almost two-thirds of all online time by 2023.

In 2015 social media took up a quarter of people's time online, but by 2023 this had risen to 40%, the largest share on either chart. Video streaming showed a similar pattern, growing from 15% to a quarter, and online shopping increased more modestly, from 10% to 15%.

The two remaining categories moved in the opposite direction. Reading news and looking for information, which had been the biggest activity in 2015 at 30%, fell to just 12% eight years later. The decline in email and work-related use was even steeper in relative terms, from a fifth of online time to only 8%.

**Common mistakes in pie charts:**
▸ "The pie chart increased" - a pie does not grow; the **share** of a **segment** grows.
▸ Saying "which was 100%" or adding up the segments to prove the total.
▸ rose/fell on a single pie (with no time comparison) - write is the largest, accounts for.
▸ Percentage point: 25% → 40% is "a rise of 15 percentage points", not "15 percent".
▸ One whole pie, then the other whole pie - always compare the two pies segment by segment.

chapters.title: Combination - two different visuals together
blocks: Sometimes you are given two visuals - for example a bar chart (total numbers) and a pie chart (the breakdown for one year), or a map + a table. The rules:
The introduction covers both visuals, in one or two sentences.
The overview gives one main point from each visual.

One body paragraph for each visual. Make comparisons within the same visual; do not compare across the two visuals - unless the question itself links them (e.g. the pie is the breakdown of the bar chart's last year - then you can link them).
Give the two roughly equal words. Many students spend everything on the first visual and write two lines on the second.
The bar chart shows the number of visitors to the National Science Museum from 2015 to 2020, and the pie chart shows where these visitors came from in 2020.
Visitors to the National Science Museum · Where 2020 visitors came from
Bar: rose for five years in a row (420 → 600), then a collapse in 2020 (210 - one third of 2019).
Pie: of the 2020 visitors, 55% local, 30% from elsewhere in the country, 15% foreign → 85% domestic.
The two visuals are linked (pie = the 2020 bar), so you can say "of those 210,000…".

The bar chart records annual attendance at the National Science Museum from 2015 to 2020, while the pie chart shows the breakdown of the 2020 audience by place of origin.

Overall, five consecutive years of growth were abruptly reversed in 2020, when visitor numbers fell to their lowest level of the period. That diminished audience was overwhelmingly domestic, with residents of the host city alone accounting for more than half of all visits.

Attendance rose without interruption from 420,000 in 2015 to 600,000 in 2019, a cumulative increase of 43%. Growth was most rapid in the middle of the period, with gains of around 50,000 to 60,000 a year in 2017 and 2018, before slowing slightly in 2019. The following year saw a dramatic collapse to 210,000, roughly a third of the 2019 peak and half the 2015 starting figure.

Of these visitors, 55% were local and a further 30% travelled from other parts of the country, meaning that domestic visitors made up 85% of the total. International tourists represented the remaining 15%, equivalent to a little over 30,000 people.

Notice the last paragraph: 15% × 210,000 ≈ 31,500 - the two visuals have been linked correctly because the pie is for that same year. But you could not write "Local visitors increased" - there is no 2015 pie, so there is no data to compare. Never write what is not in the chart; and "probably because of the pandemic" - that is opinion, forbidden.
Before writing, marked the highest, the lowest, the biggest change and the exceptions.
Overview has the leader and the main pattern, without numbers.
Arranged the data by behaviour, not in reading order.
Wherever possible, expressed numbers as relationships (double, a third, level with).
Pie: compared the pies segment by segment; words of proportion; rose/fell only for comparisons over time.
Combination: each visual has its own paragraph; cross-comparison only if the question links them; words shared equally.
No opinion, no information from outside the chart.

chapters.title: Part C - Flow Chart (Process) · Cycle · Diagram
blocks: These types have no numbers. So there is no trend either. Here you describe stages (process), parts and how they relate (diagram), or changes to a place (map). The paragraph template is the same: introduction → overview → two body paragraphs.
Flow Chart / Process - step by step
How many stages are there? Where does it start, where does it end?
Linear (start → end) or cycle (the end returns to the start)?
Man-made (a factory process) or natural (the water cycle, an animal's life cycle)?
Are there clear sections (segments)? If so, each section is one body paragraph.
Which labels are nouns that need to be turned into verbs? ("crushing" → is crushed)
Present simple (there are usually no years).
Man-made process → passive (the beans are roasted). Natural process → active (water evaporates).
First / To begin with · Next · Then · After that · Once this is complete · At the following stage · Subsequently · Meanwhile · In the final stage · Finally

is collected, sorted, cleaned, washed, mixed, heated, cooled, pressed, dried, cut, packed, transported, stored, filtered, separated · is converted into · passes through · is fed into · is removed / added
in order to · so that · which allows / enables … to …
The diagram shows how olive oil is produced.
9 stages, linear (harvesting → bottling), man-made, so passive + present.
Natural division: stages 1–5 = preparing and crushing the olives; stages 6–9 = separating and packing the oil. → two body paragraphs.
From label to verb: harvesting → are harvested; washing → are washed; crushing → are crushed; mixing → is stirred; bottling → is bottled.
In a process introduction, say: what is produced / how it works + how many stages.
The diagram illustrates the nine stages involved in turning freshly picked olives into bottled olive oil.
In the overview: linear or cycle, natural or man-made, how many main phases, what the start and end are.
Overall, this is a linear, man-made process in three main phases: the olives are first cleaned, then crushed and mixed to release the oil, and finally the oil is separated, filtered and packaged.

The process begins when olives are harvested from the trees between October and December. Any leaves and twigs are removed, and the fruit is washed. The clean olives are then crushed into a thick paste, which is stirred slowly for about thirty minutes so that the tiny drops of oil combine into larger ones.

Next, the paste is placed in a centrifuge, which spins it at high speed to separate the oil from the water and solid matter. The oil that comes out is filtered to remove any remaining particles and stored in stainless steel tanks. In the final stage, it is poured into bottles, ready for sale.

(163 words including the intro/overview. Notice: every stage is passive; variety in the sequencers - begins when, then, which, next, in the final stage; "so that the tiny drops…" - you can write this if it is in the diagram's labels, not if it isn't.)

**Common mistakes in a process:**
▸ Adding information that is not in the diagram (what temperature, how long) - only if it is in a label.
▸ Explaining why a stage happens, if the diagram does not say.
▸ Trend words (increase, decrease) - there are no numbers.
▸ "Then… Then… Then…" - vary the sequencers.
▸ Leaving out the overview - state the number of stages, the start, the end, whether it is a cycle.
Cycle - a life cycle or a natural cycle

A cycle has no real "start". So choose a logical starting point (evaporation in the water cycle; the egg for an insect), say clearly that it is a cycle, and join the last stage back to the first. Natural process → active voice, present simple.
The diagram shows the life cycle of a butterfly.

The diagram illustrates the four stages in the life of a butterfly, from egg to adult.

Overall, this is a natural, continuous cycle in which an egg develops through a feeding stage and a resting stage into an adult insect, which in turn produces new eggs, so the process never ends.

The cycle begins when an adult butterfly lays its eggs on the leaf of a plant. After a few days, a caterpillar hatches from each egg and spends the following two to three weeks eating leaves and growing rapidly. Once it is fully grown, the caterpillar attaches itself to a stem and forms a hard protective case known as a chrysalis.

Inside this case, over a period of roughly two weeks, the insect's body is completely transformed. Eventually an adult butterfly breaks out of the chrysalis. Finally, the adult finds a mate and lays eggs of its own on a fresh leaf, and the cycle begins again.

Notice: active voice (lays, hatches, spends, attaches, breaks out); returning to the start with "and the cycle begins again"; the time information (two to three weeks, two weeks) comes from the diagram's labels.
A diagram shows the parts of a machine or system and how they are connected. It is just like a process, but along with the order you also have to state the position.
The language of parts and position
consists of · is made up of · comprises · has three main parts
is attached to · is connected to · is linked to · is mounted on · is fitted with · runs from … to …
is located above / below / beside / inside / on top of · at the base of · to the left / right of · in the centre
flows through · passes through · enters / exits at · is fed into · is pumped / carried / channelled to · rises / falls
which allows … to · so that · in order to · this prevents / ensures …
The diagram shows how a rainwater harvesting system works in a school.
Rainwater harvesting system for a school
Parts: roof → gutter → downpipe (leaf filter) → first-flush diverter → underground tank (10,000 L) → pump → overhead tank → toilets & garden taps; overflow pipe → drain.
There is an order following the path of the water, so we write it like a process; plus where each thing is (underground, overhead, on the roof).
Two body paragraphs: (1) collection and cleaning (roof → tank), (2) storage and use (tank → taps).

The diagram illustrates the components of a rainwater collection system installed at a school and shows how rain falling on the roof is stored and reused.

Overall, water is collected from the roof, cleaned in two stages, stored in an underground tank and then pumped to a rooftop tank, from which it supplies the school's toilets and garden taps.

Rain that lands on the sloping roof runs into a gutter along its edge and then down a vertical pipe fitted with a filter that catches leaves. Below this, a device known as a first-flush diverter sends the first, dirtiest water to the drain and allows the rest to continue into a 10,000-litre tank buried underground.

When water is needed, an electric pump located beside the tank lifts it through a pipe to a smaller tank on the roof of the building. From there it flows by gravity to the toilets and the garden taps. If the underground tank becomes full, an overflow pipe carries the excess water to the drain.
If the task has two designs (e.g. two kinds of bridge or two kinds of foundation), describe each one briefly and then compare them - the differences are then the main feature.

chapters.title: Map - step by step
blocks: The same place, two times (most common)
Past (was built), or present perfect (has been built) if the second map is "today/now"
The current situation + a proposed plan
What is there now, what will happen under the plan
Present + future (will be / is to be / is going to be built)
Two possible locations (site A, site B)
Compare the features of the two sites (distance, access, size)
Find the compass (usually north is at the top). Find landmarks that appear on both maps (a river, the main road) - you need these to give directions.
Make a list: what has disappeared, what is new, what has changed in size or use, what is unchanged.
Group the changes: by area (north/south, centre/edge) or by type (housing, transport, green areas).
Overview = the overall character of the change: more built-up / larger / more modern / farmland turned into housing / expanded eastwards.

was built / constructed / added / extended / enlarged / expanded · was demolished / removed / knocked down / cleared / cut down · was replaced by / converted into / turned into / redeveloped as · was relocated / moved to

in the north-east corner · along the river / coast · on the western edge · on the outskirts · adjacent to · next to · opposite · in the centre · on the site of the old … · to the south of · running from north to south · across the road from
remained / was retained / was kept / stayed in place / was unchanged / still exists
doubled in size · was reduced by half · now covers … · a much larger …
Example - the same place, two times
The maps show the coastal town of Seabrook in 1980 and today.
farmland (in the south); half of the forest
hotels (on the beach); housing estate; shopping centre; ring road; golf course; ferry terminal
main road; houses; beach; the rest of the forest
Groups: (1) the coast and harbour (east/north-east), (2) the south and the centre. Overview: small fishing village → large tourist and residential town; the main road and the old houses remain.

The two maps show how the coastal town of Seabrook has developed since 1980.

Overall, the town has grown from a small fishing settlement into a much larger tourist and residential centre. Most of the change has taken place along the coast and on the former farmland to the south, while the original main road and the houses beside it have been kept.

The greatest transformation is along the eastern shore. The beach, which in 1980 was undeveloped, is now lined with hotels, and the fishing harbour in the north-east has been extended to include a ferry terminal.

South of the main road, the farmland has disappeared completely and has been replaced by a housing estate and a shopping centre, served by a new ring road that curves around the southern edge of the town. In the south-west, about half of the forest has been cut down to make way for a golf course. In the centre, the school has been enlarged to roughly twice its original size, but the original houses along the main road remain as they were.

Notice: (1) the 1980 map is not described separately - only the changes; (2) a direction in every sentence (eastern shore, north-east, south of, south-west, in the centre); (3) present perfect because of "today" (has been extended, has disappeared); (4) the unchanged things are mentioned too.

**Common mistakes in maps:**
▸ All of map 1, then all of map 2 - that is two inventories, not a comparison.
▸ Tense: a map of the past → past; a plan → future (will be built / is to be built).
▸ Not giving directions - reading "there is a school and a road", the reader understands nothing.
▸ Forgetting the unchanged things - "what has stayed the same" is part of the overview.
▸ "The town developed because tourists came" - the reason is not in the chart; it is opinion.
Process: number of stages, start and end, linear/cycle - in the overview.
Process: present simple; man-made → passive, natural → active; variety in sequencers.
Diagram: names of the parts, position, order of the flow.
Map: the changes (not two inventories); compass directions; mention the unchanged things.
Added nothing that is not in the visual; no opinion.
