chapters.title: Part A - Ground rules and recognising the question type
blocks: Task 2 is an essay. In the Writing band it carries twice the weight of Task 1 - so give it more of all three: time, care and practice.
Rule: minimum 250 words. There is no upper limit, so the same question arises - how much should I write? Answer: 260–290, 300 at most.
Never below 250. Even 248 words is a penalty.
There is no gain above 320; mistakes simply increase and revision time is lost.
The space on the answer sheet easily holds 280 words. If you need to ask for an extra sheet, you know you are writing too much.
Every word counts (see the Task 1 rules). Words copied from the question are no proof of your skill.
Do not count in the exam hall; know beforehand how many lines 280 words take in your handwriting (usually 18–22).
Read the question twice, underline, decide the type, brainstorm, plan

The question paper itself says 40 minutes; some take a little more, some less, but keep it to 40 on average. Those who skip the plan end up with a paragraph that loses direction; those who skip revision leave five easy mistakes behind. Each costs half a band.

The standard is 5: Introduction · Body 1 · Body 2 · Body 3 · Conclusion. Writing 4 (two body paragraphs) gets the same score, if the ideas are well developed. What will not work: one huge block, or seven or eight two-line fragments.
No **heading**, no bullets, no numbering in any paragraph. Full sentences, full paragraphs.

Task 2 topics are always about society: education, work, technology, environment, health, family, crime, cities, media, culture - their causes, results, solutions, advantages and disadvantages, or an opinion on some controversial issue. No topic needs specialised knowledge, so there is nothing to fear. But general knowledge is definitely needed - every point needs a reason and an example, and they have to come out of your own head. So reading the news in English every day is, in fact, exam preparation.
What to make sure of in Task 2 (must-list)
In a paper test, write in pencil - corrections are easy.
Read the whole question twice. Underline the subject words (the topic) and the instruction words (what you must do) separately.
Decide the question type (below). This is what decides what goes in the conclusion.

Brainstorm in the blank space on the question paper - 3–5 points for each side. This is 70% of the essay's work; the IELTS authority itself says up to 8 minutes can be given to brainstorming, we would say at least 5.
At the end, check your writing for 3–5 minutes - you will catch many of your own mistakes yourself.
Repeating the words of the question where a synonym exists.

Writing anything irrelevant. One sentence is forgiven, one paragraph is not - say the topic is child education: you can write a sentence or two about adult education, but a whole paragraph will be marked irrelevant and your score will drop.

Using grammar or words you are not sure of. If you make mistakes while trying to use varied sentences and uncommon vocabulary, instead of rising, your score falls below what you would normally get. Only if you are confident; otherwise write simple sentences of the "I eat rice" type and join them with linking words.
Memorised essays. The examiner recognises them at a glance, and a memorised essay never fits the actual question.
Writing until the last moment - without revision.
The bottom line: organise the essay properly and present your point of view clearly. That is what gets a good score.
Recognising the question type - the most important skill
Every Task 2 question has two parts:
Statement / topic - what the subject is.

Instruction - what you must do with the subject. This is usually the last sentence. (The general instruction underneath it - "Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples…" - appears in every question; that is not what we mean.)
Read the instruction first. The same topic can become two different tasks:

A. Computers have become a part and parcel of modern life. What are the advantages and disadvantages of using a computer?
B. Computers have become a part and parcel of modern life, but their demerits outweigh their merits. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

On a first reading the two seem the same. Read again - the first part is the same, the difference is in the second part, and that difference decides which type each one is. A asks you to describe both sides; no opinion of your own is needed. B asks you to take a side and argue for it.
The key difference: freedom of choice
There is only one key difference between the two families of questions - freedom of choice.
None - the question itself tells you what to write
Yes - you may choose either side
Only what is asked - causes, problems, advantages and disadvantages, solutions
Arguments for both sides, then your own side
No (unless the question asks); a suggestion can be given
Definitely - in the introduction and conclusion
There is a third type - Combination - where one task contains both. Below is how to recognise each, with examples.
How to recognise a narrative task
1. A question with the topic whose answer is a number of points
Example 1: Fewer young people are choosing to become teachers. Why do you think this is happening?
The answer to the question is a set of points: (1) low salary, (2) heavy workload, (3) better-paid alternatives… There is no side - you only have to write why fewer are choosing it. → Narrative.
2. When the topic contains these words
advantages / disadvantages · pros / cons · benefits / drawbacks · merits / demerits
problems / solutions · measures · what can be done
N.B. Both will not always be there. Only advantages, only problems, only causes - these also come. Write only what is asked.

Example 2: Tourism is becoming increasingly important as a source of revenue for many countries, but its problems should not be overlooked. What are the problems of tourism?
→ Narrative. Only problems. A paragraph on the benefits of tourism would be irrelevant.
Example 3: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of children using smartphones.
→ Narrative. Both sides, kept in balance; no opinion has been asked for.
Example 4: More and more people are living alone. What are the causes of this trend, and what effects does it have on society?
→ Narrative, two parts: causes + effects.
Example 5: Traffic congestion is worsening in most large cities. What problems does this cause, and what measures could reduce it?
→ Narrative, two parts: problems + solutions (give suggestions, not an opinion).

Example 6: Children should be sent to kindergarten before starting primary school. Discuss.
→ Narrative. You have to write the reasons why they should be sent; not for and against. (But when "Discuss" is there, it is safe to touch briefly on the other side.)
How to recognise an argumentative task

Example 7: Some people believe they should keep all the money they earn and should not pay tax to the state. Do you agree or disagree?
Example 8: Air travel should be restricted because it causes serious pollution and uses up the world's fuel resources. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
→ Both are argumentative. For or against - your choice. Even with only "Do you agree?" (even if "disagree" is not written) it is argumentative, and you must write the arguments of both sides.
2. A question whose answer is yes or no

Example 9: Should companies hire employees for their entire working lives?
Example 10: Is education more important than anything else for success in life?
Example 11: Do children today need more time for recreation?
→ Each answer is yes/no - you choose. Argumentative.

Example 12: Some people think teachers should be responsible for a child's overall development. Others believe teachers should only teach academic subjects. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
→ Argumentative. The two sides in separate paragraphs, then which side you are on.
4. When only an opinion / view is asked for

Example 13: Some countries have banned smoking in all public places. What is your opinion?
→ Argumentative - if your view is asked for, you must take a side.

Example 14: Should education continue throughout a person's life? Give reasons.
→ The answer to the question is yes/no, so there is freedom of choice - argumentative. (The same if it says "Discuss".)

Example 15: More people are working from home. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
Example 16: Many people now shop online instead of in local stores. Is this a positive or negative development?
→ Although the words look narrative, outweigh and positive or negative ask for a verdict. Argumentative - both sides, then the verdict.

Example 17: Reading on the internet is taking over the conventional way of reading.
→ Add "Do you agree or disagree?" yourself - you will see it has become argumentative. If only a statement comes in the exam, it is definitely argumentative.
How to recognise a combination task
Two questions or statements in one task, on the same topic. This does not come very often, but if you are prepared you will not panic when it does. Usually one is narrative and one argumentative.

Example 18: There are social, medical and technical problems associated with the use of mobile phones. What forms do they take? Do you agree that the problems outweigh the benefits of mobile phones?
→ The first question (what forms) - the answer is a set of points, no choice → narrative. The second (do you agree … outweigh) - there is a choice → argumentative.
Example 19: An increasing number of people are choosing not to own a car. Why might this be? Do you think it is a good idea?
→ Reasons (narrative) + opinion (argumentative).
Example 20: Fewer people are cooking at home. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?
→ Reasons (narrative) + verdict (argumentative).
⚠ In a combination task both questions must be answered, in separate paragraphs. Leaving one out is the most common reason good writers get stuck at Band 6.
At a glance - the type from the instruction
To what extent do you agree or disagree? / Do you agree?
Discuss both views and give your opinion
Do the advantages outweigh the disadvantages?
Is this a positive or negative development?
What are the advantages and disadvantages?
What are the causes / effects / problems?
The key difference between argumentative and narrative - in one line

**Argumentative:** whichever side you are on, you must write the arguments of both sides; the conclusion must have an **opinion**, with a suggestion too if you wish.
**Narrative:** only what the task asks for; in the conclusion only a **suggestion** can be given - there is no rule to give an opinion.
1. Many people believe zoos should be closed. To what extent do you agree?
2. What are the causes of childhood obesity, and what can be done to reduce it?
3. Some think university should be free; others think students should pay. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
4. More people are working from home. Why is this? Is it a positive or negative development?
5. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of international tourism.
6. Advertising aimed at children is harmful.
7. Should governments spend money on space exploration?
8. What problems does traffic congestion cause in big cities?
9. Many museums charge for admission while others are free. Do you think the advantages of charging outweigh the disadvantages?
10. Some people prefer to live in a house, others in a flat. What are the benefits of each?
Answers: 1 A · 2 N (causes + solutions) · 3 A · 4 C · 5 N · 6 A (only a statement) · 7 A (yes/no) · 8 N (only problems) · 9 A (outweigh) · 10 N (benefits of both, no opinion)

chapters.title: Part B - The argumentative essay step by step: from topic to introduction
blocks: Now let us get to the main work. How an argumentative essay can be taken step by step in the exam hall, from thinking to finished writing, is shown in full using one question. Follow the steps in order; in the hall, 5 minutes for planning and 30 for writing.

Suppose this task has come up in your exam:
Some people believe that private cars should be banned from city centres. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Analyse the topic properly and understand it. This has a few steps:
1.1 Say the task in your own words (in Bangla)
"Private cars should be banned from the centre of the city - how far do I agree with this view?"
1.2 Separate out the subject matter (the core parts)

Write the important parts of the task separately on the question paper, because the essay will be about these parts. Here: private cars · city centres · banned. Notice that the rest of the topic ("some people believe") is of no use for the writing - it is just wrapping.
1.3 Think about the inside of each part
Understand the meaning of each piece of subject matter separately and how they relate to each other - this gives you an in-depth idea of the topic:
"Private cars" - not buses, taxis or delivery vans. So people can still get around after a ban.
"City centres" - not the whole city, only the centre. So residents can still own cars.
"Banned" - completely, or at certain times? Exemptions for elderly or disabled people?
N.B. You do not have to write all these points in the essay, but this thought process will give you a good understanding of the task and supply ideas for brainstorming.
Step 2 · Deciding the task type (10 seconds)
Seeing "To what extent do you agree or disagree?" you have surely understood - argumentative. That means: arguments for both sides, a clear opinion, the last word on your own side.
The importance of brainstorming has already been mentioned - a good brainstorm means 70% of the essay's work is done. It has a few steps:
It is argumentative, so the essay has two viewpoints: for (in favour of the ban) and against.
3.2 Write in two columns - leave nothing out

In the blank space on the question paper, below the subject matter, write For on one side and Against on the other. First think only of the For points - you do not need Against at this moment. Then do the same for Against. Write down everything that comes to mind; judge later.
At this moment the question paper looks like this:
2. Unfair to elderly and disabled people
3. Public transport not good enough in many cities
5. Traffic just moves to the edge of the centre

**Remember while brainstorming:**
▸ Do not stop until you have at least 3 points on one side or the other. Once you have 4–5 you need no more.
▸ There is no rule that both sides must have the same number of points.
▸ Write down everything task-related that comes to mind - weak ideas too. Selection comes at the next step.

Now look at the chart, see which points seem more important, and arrange them in order. Because you wrote the points down in the order they came to mind - in most cases that is not the order of importance. The best idea usually comes later.
N.B. Your order may not match mine - that is no problem; it will not differ very much.
After arranging - notice that the For and Against points have been put in one serial (1 to 7); you will see the advantage of this shortly:
6. Public transport not ready in many cities
3. Space for people: parks, markets, cafés
"People exercise more" - weak, dropped. "Delivery vehicles" - solved simply by an exemption, weak, dropped. "Traffic moves to the edge" - weak, dropped.
3.4 Choose your side - after brainstorming, not before

An argumentative essay needs an opinion, so even though you write the arguments of both sides, you must choose one side. Notice that up to now you have not chosen a side. Because choosing earlier causes two problems:
If you are on one side from the start, your thinking becomes biased - the other side's arguments do not come to mind properly.

Often the side you first thought of seems right, but what an essay needs is not what you feel but strong arguments. After brainstorming you can see which side has the stronger arguments - that will be your side, because then the essay will automatically be strong.
Here it is clear: For has more strong arguments, and every Against point has an answer. So we will agree, while acknowledging the problems.
Step 4 · Planning the body paragraphs (1 minute)

You might think that writing an essay starts with the introduction. But here we are talking about the plan - in your head - of how you will build the paragraphs from the brainstorm. It can be done in two ways:
Your side's #3, #4 - and why they outweigh Body 2

**N.B.** Do you see the advantage of arranging the brainstorm? The weak arguments have dropped out automatically, and the numbers of the points show at once which one goes in which paragraph. Whichever method you use, the body is built from 3+3 = 6 points; the extra point (#4) you can give if you like, or not. In fact **the essay has already been made in the brainstorm**; now it is only a matter of writing.

Both methods score the same. Method 1 is easier for most students; Method 2 looks a little more mature and fits "discuss both views" questions well. We will write the whole essay with Method 1, and then also show how it would go with Method 2.
Step 5 · Emphasising and softening words (Emphasisers and Softeners)
In an argumentative essay the examiner must come away feeling that you are right. Two small tools do this:
Makes the information in a sentence weightier, increases its importance - in your own side's points

clearly, undoubtedly, certainly, obviously, indeed, in fact, actually, without doubt, needless to say, it goes without saying that, the main, the most, the greatest, crucial, vital, overwhelming, solely, mainly, pivotal
Makes the information lighter, reduces its importance - in the opposing side's points
perhaps, probably, possibly, may, might, can, could, some, a few, a little, little, only, to some extent, arguably, a minority, unlikely, it is sometimes claimed that, it is said that
Although some shop owners may lose a little trade at first, a car-free centre undoubtedly attracts far more visitors in the long run.

N.B. These very words are the difference between argumentative and narrative. In narrative you need not be conscious of them - use whatever fits where. But in argumentative: emphasisers in your own points, softeners in the opposing points - every time.
Depending on the structure of the sentence, the same word can be an emphasiser or a softener:
Actually, it is not so true. - here "actually" is a softener: it reduces the importance of what was said before.
It is the least the government can do. - here "least" is an emphasiser: it puts force into the sentence ("this much at least must be done").
So look at the whole sentence, not just the word.
Step 6 · Writing the introduction (2–3 sentences, 40–55 words)
Write the introduction in 3 sentences at most, or 2. No argument comes here. Format:

1. General statement (1 sentence)
2. Thesis statement (1 sentence)

1. General statements (2 sentences)
2. Thesis statement (1 sentence)

As the first sentence (or two) of the introduction, write a general sentence that is about the subject matter of the task and relevant to the topic, but does not go into the task's argument. Build the sentence from any one or two pieces of the subject matter:
Private cars have become the main form of transport in almost every city in the world.
City centres are where the pressure of urban traffic is felt most sharply.
In recent years, a growing number of cities have begun to restrict private cars in their central districts.

The first two do not create a link between cars and city centres - so after them you need another sentence that leads into the thesis (a 3-sentence introduction). The third brings the two together - go straight to the thesis (a 2-sentence introduction). It is no problem if your sentences are simpler than these - as long as there are no mistakes.

This is the most important sentence of the task. Here you make clear which side you are on - this is what the examiner reads most carefully. A good thesis contains: your position + a hint of the main reason + (optionally) an acknowledgement of the other side with a softener:

Although such a policy creates some (softener) difficulties for businesses and less mobile residents, I firmly (emphasiser) believe that banning cars from city centres is the right decision because of the enormous gains in air quality, safety and public space.

"I agree with the topic" / "I disagree with the topic" - you can write this, it is not wrong, but it is not up to standard. Do not start with a question. Writing "This essay will discuss…" without stating your own view - that is not a thesis.
Now the third general statement + the thesis = a complete introduction (44 words):

In recent years, a growing number of cities have begun to restrict private cars in their central districts. Although such a policy creates some difficulties for businesses and less mobile residents, I firmly believe it is the right decision because of the gains in air quality, safety and public space.

Notice: "cars", "city centres" - the task's own words have been repeated. This can happen; it is no problem. But if you like, cars → vehicles, city centres → central districts / downtown areas - use a synonym if one comes to mind; if not, the same word will more or less do.
You can use this for any argumentative task by slotting in the topic. For each blank, choose any one of the words given:

Truth be told, whether or not **[insert the topic, slightly reworded]** has generated a lot of **[ interest / controversy / discussion ] [ lately / recently / in recent years ]**. The goal of this essay is to **[ clear / document / establish ]** why my answer is **[ yes / no ]**.

Example: Truth be told, whether or not private vehicles should be excluded from downtown areas has generated a lot of controversy in recent years. The goal of this essay is to establish why my answer is yes.

The **[ issue / subject / matter ]** of **[the topic, slightly reworded]** has been **[ raising eyebrows / a matter of controversy / a matter of discussion ]** for quite some time now. In my perspective, it would be hard to **[ claim / prove / show / deny ]** that **[the topic again, put differently]** is / are **[ good / bad ]** for society.
If you are for, "good"; if against, "bad"; using "deny" reverses the meaning - be careful.

**[Subject paraphrase]** has become **[ a widespread practice / a contested issue / a common feature of modern life ]**. While [the opposing view, with a **softener**], I **[ firmly / strongly ]** believe that [your **position**], **[ mainly / chiefly ]** because [the main reason].

chapters.title: Part B - The argumentative essay step by step: body, conclusion and the full essay
blocks: The structure of each paragraph under Method 1:
The paragraph's main claim in one sentence; tells the reader what is coming in the paragraph (works like an introduction)
If the topic sentence does not state the paragraph's idea fully clearly, explain in 1–2 sentences; no more
One concrete example - a country, an event, a common situation
One per paragraph; if not 3, then at least 2
Return to the thesis in one sentence
Since you are about to give the first 2 arguments for your side, the topic sentence should represent both points:

Topic sentence: The most compelling (emphasiser) reason for excluding cars is the effect on the environment of the city itself.
Explanation (point #1): Undoubtedly (emphasiser), private vehicles are the main (emphasiser) source of air pollution and noise in central areas, and removing them brings almost immediate relief.
Point #2: Moreover (adding connective), buses and trams that no longer sit in traffic jams become faster and more reliable, so (resulting connective) more people choose them.
Example: For instance (connective), when Oslo removed most cars from its centre, nitrogen dioxide levels dropped sharply within two years and bus journey times fell by a fifth. (84 words)

**[ Undoubtedly / Obviously / Without a hint of doubt / It is undisputed that / It is beyond argument that ]**, the **[ basic / fundamental / main / pivotal ] [ reasons / factors / grounds / causes ]** for which **[topic]** is/are important is/are **[the first 1/2 points from the brainstorm]**. **[ Firstly / At first / To begin with ]**, … (a little explanation). For example, … (example). Moreover, … (1 sentence if there is another point).

Start the paragraph with a contrasting connective (however, on the other hand, on the contrary, in contrast). Softeners on the opposing points. Everything else as in the previous paragraph. At the end, hint in one sentence that these points have an answer.

Topic sentence: On the other hand (contrasting connective), opponents raise some (softener) concerns worth taking seriously.
Point #5: Shop owners may (softener) fear losing customers who arrive by car, and elderly or disabled residents could (softener) find a car-free centre harder to reach.
Point #6: It is also sometimes claimed that (softener) public transport in many cities is not yet (softener) good enough to replace private vehicles.
Hint of the answer: However (contrasting), these problems are practical rather than fundamental: exemptions for people with limited mobility and a phased introduction alongside transport investment have solved them wherever they have been tried. (86 words)

N.B. Notice that Against #7 (shops lose customers) has not been developed separately here - it has only been touched on with "shop owners may fear", because the paragraph was getting long and the answer to that point will come in Body 3. In the exam, do the same if you need to.

**[ However / On the contrary / On the other hand / In contrast ]**, it is **[ argued that / not possible to deny that ] [topic]** has its **[ downsides / negatives / negative sides / drawbacks / disadvantages ]**. **[ Firstly / At first / To begin with ]**, … (the first opposing point, a little explanation). Secondly, … (2nd point). Finally, … (3rd). For instance, … (example).
Body para 3 - your side again (#3, #4) and why it wins
At the start of this paragraph, again a contrasting connective, then as before. Since this is the last body paragraph, this is where you show that your side outweighs the other.

Topic sentence: Furthermore (adding connective - back to your own side after answering Body 2), a ban frees an enormous (emphasiser) amount of space for people rather than machines.
Explanation (#3, #4): Roads and car parks can become markets, cafés, cycle lanes and small parks, which makes the centre safer and far (emphasiser) more pleasant to visit.
Example + answer to opposing #7: In fact (emphasiser), this is why the fear of empty shops proves unfounded: pedestrianised streets in cities such as Copenhagen record more (emphasiser) visitors and higher retail sales than the car-filled streets they replaced, because people linger, walk and browse instead of driving through. (90 words)

**[ However / On the contrary / On the other hand / In contrast ]**, there are **[ more / many other / so many more / a myriad of / numerous ] [ reasons / factors / grounds / causes / variables ]** why **[topic]** is so crucial. **[ Firstly / At first / To begin with ]**, let us talk about **[the next 1/2 points for your side]**. … (a little explanation). Then, … (if there is another point). To exemplify, … (example).

**Some essential information:**
▸ The introduction and conclusion templates are the same for both methods. The body paragraph templates differ between the two methods.
▸ You can freely use connectives / linking phrases from outside these templates too (the list in Chapter 1).
▸ Never, ever give any paragraph a heading.
▸ A template is a skeleton - it must be filled with content from your own topic; if you hand in a bare template, the examiner will spot it.
The body with Method 2 - the same essay, a different layout

In this method each paragraph first gives a little of the opposing view, then your argument. The opposing view needs no example. The introduction and conclusion stay the same; only the layout of the body changes. See how exactly the same sentences fit into the new mould:

It is often argued that (softener) a car-free centre would be unfair to elderly and disabled residents who cannot walk far. However (contrasting connector), exemptions for people with limited mobility are simple to arrange, and the gain for everyone else is enormous (emphasiser): private vehicles are undoubtedly the main source of air pollution and noise in central areas, and removing them brings almost immediate relief. For instance, when Oslo removed most cars from its centre, nitrogen dioxide levels dropped sharply within two years. (83 words)

It is **[ argued / said / claimed / observed ]** that / It is not possible to overlook that **[topic] [the first opposing point]**. **[ However / On the other hand / But / On the contrary ]**, **[ it is undisputed / it is needless to say / it is beyond argument / it goes without saying ]** that **[the first point for your side]**. … (explanation in one more sentence). For example, … (example).

Some people can say (softener) that public transport in most cities is not yet good enough to replace the car. On the contrary (contrasting), the ban itself is what makes public transport work: buses and trams that no longer sit in traffic jams become faster and more reliable, so more people choose them. In Oslo, bus journey times fell by a fifth within two years of the restrictions. (72 words)
Template: the same as the previous template, only with the 2nd opposing point in place of the 1st, and the 2nd point for your side.

Finally, there is a slight (softener) possibility that shops in the centre will lose customers who used to arrive by car. However, it is outweighed by (emphasiser) the space a ban frees for people rather than machines: roads and car parks become markets, cafés and cycle lanes, and the centre becomes safer and more pleasant. In fact, pedestrianised streets in cities such as Copenhagen record more visitors and higher retail sales than the car-filled streets they replaced. (81 words)

Finally, there is a **[ marginal / slight / minimal / slim / faint ] [ possibility / chance ]** that **[the part of the topic the last opposing point is about]**. … (explanation in one sentence). **[ However / On the other hand / But / On the contrary ]**, it is / they are outweighed by **[the last point for your side]**. … (explanation in one sentence, or write "to stress the matter up," and go straight to an example).
The body paragraphs are done. As simple as that!
Step 8 · Writing the conclusion (1–2 sentences, 30–45 words)
Here you will of course give your opinion (firmly, which side you are on), and a suggestion as well if you like. Paragraph format:
A concluding connective (in conclusion, to sum up, in sum, to conclude…).
Your opinion - these two together make one sentence.

In conclusion, while a car ban brings short-term inconvenience for some, its benefits for health, mobility and the life of the city are far greater, and city authorities should introduce it gradually together with better public transport. (37 words)
See - a one-sentence conclusion, with opinion + suggestion.

**What not to do in the conclusion:** bring in a new argument · copy the thesis word for word (paraphrase it) · suddenly turn "balanced" at the end of a one-sided essay · end with a question · "Thank you" · start with "Last but not least".

What I have argued here is that **[thesis statement** in brief, slightly reworded**]**. **[ However / On the other hand / But / On the contrary ]**, I cannot **[ say / offer the comforting assurance ]** that it is not without **[ limitations / lopsidedness / downsides / drawbacks ]**.

I have no illusions that my claim will be **[ palatable to all / acceptable to all / easy to all ]**. **[ However / On the other hand / But / On the contrary ]**, I hope that my **[ analysis / exploration / argument ]** can help to understand the matter better.
In conclusion, although [the strongest opposing point, with a **softener**], [your **position** in other words]; **[suggestion /** its result**]**.
The emphasising and softening words and the connectives are shown in bold:

In recent years, a growing number of cities have begun to restrict private cars in their central districts. Although such a policy creates **some** negative aspects for businesses and less mobile residents, I **firmly** believe it is the right decision because of the gains in air quality, safety and public space.

The **most compelling** reason for excluding cars is the effect on the environment of the city itself. **Undoubtedly**, private vehicles are the **main** source of air pollution and noise in central areas, and removing them brings almost immediate relief. **Moreover**, buses and trams that no longer sit in traffic jams become faster and more reliable, **so** more people choose them. **For instance**, when Oslo removed most cars from its centre, nitrogen dioxide levels dropped sharply within two years and bus journey times fell by a fifth.

**On the other hand**, opponents raise **some** concerns worth taking seriously. Shop owners **may** fear losing customers who arrive by car, and elderly or disabled residents **could** find a car-free centre harder to reach. **It is also sometimes claimed that** public transport in many cities is **not yet** good enough to replace private vehicles. **However**, these problems are practical rather than fundamental: exemptions for people with limited mobility and a phased introduction alongside transport investment have solved them wherever they have been tried.

**Furthermore**, a ban frees an **enormous** amount of space for people rather than machines. Roads and car parks can become markets, cafés, cycle lanes and small parks, which makes the centre safer and **far** more pleasant to visit. **In fact**, this is why the fear of empty shops proves unfounded: pedestrianised streets in cities such as Copenhagen record **more** visitors and higher retail sales than the car-filled streets they replaced.

**In conclusion**, while a car ban brings short-term inconvenience for **some**, its benefits for health, mobility and the life of the city are **far** greater, and city authorities should introduce it gradually together with better public transport.
I have identified the instruction; brainstormed both sides; taken a side on the strength of the arguments.
Introduction: general statement + a clear thesis; no argument yet.
Every body paragraph: topic sentence → explanation → example; one idea only.
Emphasisers for my side, softeners for the other side.
I have presented the other side and answered it.
Conclusion: the position in new words; nothing new.
The key noun no more than twice in a paragraph; no double connectors.
Next part: narrative and combination essays step by step.

chapters.title: Part C - The narrative essay step by step
blocks: The argumentative essay (Part B) is the hardest. A narrative essay needs the same building blocks (topic sentence, explanation, example, connectives), only with less argument and more explanation. A combination essay joins the two.
There is nothing to choose. The question itself tells you what to write: advantages, disadvantages, causes, effects, problems, solutions, reasons.
No, unless the question asks for one. A suggestion can be given at the end.
Not needed - you are explaining, not trying to persuade. Neutral language.
The same: 4–5 paragraphs, topic sentence + explanation + example, connectives, no repetition.
Solutions - each one matched to a problem

**Golden rule:** only what has been asked. If the question is "What are the problems of tourism?", a paragraph on benefits is off-topic - one band lost.
**Matching rule:** in a problem–solution essay every solution must fix a problem you have stated. Problem: cheap fast food → solution: a tax or labelling; not "build more gyms".
Step by step - a complete example
Many young people are leaving rural areas to live in cities. What are the causes of this trend, and what effects does it have on rural communities?

Subject matter: young people · rural areas → cities · causes · effects on rural communities. Two parts: causes (why they go) and effects (on the villages - not on the cities; read the question carefully).
"What are the causes … what effects …" → narrative, two parts, no opinion.
Better colleges and training in cities
Schools, clinics and shops close for lack of people
Money sent home helps families (one positive effect)
Arranged: causes - jobs, education, lifestyle (income goes inside jobs). Effects - ageing/labour shortage, services closing, traditions; and remittances - a mixed effect, good for showing balance.
Intro → Body 1 causes → Body 2 effects → Conclusion (summary + one suggestion).
General statement + one sentence on what the essay will do - not an opinion:

Across the developing world, villages are emptying of their young as they move to towns and cities in search of a better life. This essay looks at the main reasons behind this migration and at what it means for the communities left behind. (44 words)

**[Subject paraphrase]** is now **[ a growing concern / a common trend / a widespread phenomenon ]** in many **[ countries / cities / societies ]**. This essay **[ examines / outlines / identifies ]** the main **[ causes / reasons / problems ]** behind it and **[ the effects it has / suggests some measures to tackle it / considers its advantages and disadvantages ]**.

Topic sentence: The most important cause is economic.
Explanation: Rural areas usually offer little work beyond agriculture, and farming income is uncertain because it depends on the weather and on crop prices that the farmer cannot control. Cities, by contrast, provide factory, service and office jobs with a regular wage.
Cause 2: A second reason is education: colleges and vocational training are concentrated in urban centres, so anyone who wants to study beyond secondary school has to leave.
Cause 3: Finally, the attractions of city life itself, from entertainment to fast internet, pull young people who have grown up seeing that world on their phones.
Example: In Bangladesh, for example, garment factories around Dhaka have drawn hundreds of thousands of village teenagers for exactly these reasons. (118 words)

Topic sentence: The effects on the villages are mostly negative.
Effect 1: When the young leave, the remaining population ages, and there are fewer hands to work the land, so fields are sometimes abandoned.
Effect 2 (+ chain): As families shrink, local schools, clinics and shops lose the customers they need and close, which makes the village even less attractive and speeds up the cycle.
Effect 3: Traditional skills and festivals also fade, because there is no one to inherit them.
Balance: One effect is positive, however: migrants often send money home, and this income builds houses, pays school fees and keeps some rural families out of poverty. (103 words)

In conclusion, young people leave the countryside mainly for work, education and lifestyle, and their departure leaves villages older, poorer in services and weaker in culture, though partly compensated by the money sent back. Governments could slow the trend by bringing training centres and non-farm jobs to rural districts. (49 words)
About 290 words in total. Notice: a neutral tone; both parts complete; one balancing point (remittances); a suggestion at the end, but no opinion on whether migration is good or bad.
In conclusion, [a summary of part 1 in one **phrase**], and [a summary of part 2]. **[ Governments / Schools / Individuals ]** could **[ reduce / address / ease ]** this by [one **suggestion**].
The main / primary / underlying cause is … · This is largely because … · A further factor is … · This can be attributed to … · One reason is that …
As a result / Consequently, … · This leads to / results in / gives rise to … · The most serious consequence is … · One knock-on effect is …
The chief benefit is … · Another advantage is that … · This allows / enables … · Those in favour point to …
The main drawback is … · A further problem is … · This can result in … · There is a risk that …
One effective measure would be to … · Governments should / could … · This problem can be addressed by … · Another practical step is …
However, not every effect is negative. · On the positive side, … · Admittedly, …
Two more narrative moulds in brief
In many countries, more employees are working from home rather than in an office. What are the advantages and disadvantages of this trend?

Plan: Intro (trend + "this essay considers both sides") → Body 1 advantages (no commute: time & money; flexibility for parents; employers save space) → Body 2 disadvantages (isolation; work spills into every hour; not every home is suitable) → Conclusion (a summary of both sides; if you like, "a hybrid arrangement may suit most" - this is a suggestion, not an opinion). One sentence of explanation for each point; one example in each body paragraph (e.g. two hours a day saved from Dhaka's traffic jams).
The amount of plastic waste produced in the world is increasing every year. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?

Plan: Intro → Body 1 causes (single-use packaging cheap & everywhere; weak collection/recycling in many cities) → Body 2 solutions, each one answering a cause (packaging → tax/ban on thin bags, producer responsibility; weak collection → invest in door-to-door collection & sorting plants; + education campaign) → Conclusion (summary + which measure is most urgent). Examples: Bangladesh's polythene ban, Kenya's ban, Germany's deposit-return scheme.

chapters.title: Part C - The combination (two-question) essay step by step
blocks: The task contains two questions. Usually one is narrative (Why? What problems? What forms?) and one argumentative (Is it positive or negative? Do you agree?). Sometimes both are narrative (What are the causes? What can be done?) - then it is really a problem–solution essay.
Answer both, each in its own body paragraph (or two).
Mention both parts in the introduction; close both in the conclusion - with your opinion for the argumentative part.
Neutral language in the narrative part; emphasisers/softeners in the argumentative part.
General statement + one sentence covering both questions (if there is an argumentative part, your view goes right there)
Answer to question 1 (narrative) - 2–3 points, one example
Answer to question 2 - if an opinion: position + reasons + example, the other side briefly acknowledged
A second paragraph for whichever part needs more
Part 1 in one phrase, your view on part 2 again
Step by step - a complete example
An increasing number of people are choosing not to own a car. Why might this be? Do you think it is a good idea?
Part 1: reasons (narrative). Part 2: "do you think it is a good idea" → argumentative, an opinion is needed.
Good public transport, ride-hailing apps in cities
But - families with small children may need one
→ My view: good idea in cities
Notice the opinion: "yes, but in cities" - a clear view with a condition. This is not fence-sitting; rather it is an honest and strong position.

For much of the last century, owning a car was a mark of adulthood and success, yet today many people are deliberately choosing to live without one. This essay explains the main reasons for this change and argues that, at least for city dwellers, it is a sensible choice. (50 words)
Both questions in one sentence: "explains the main reasons" (part 1) + "argues that … it is a sensible choice" (part 2, with the view).

**[General statement on the subject]**. This essay **[ explains / examines / outlines ] [ why this is happening / the main reasons for this ]** and **[ argues that … / considers whether … is a positive development / suggests how … ]**.

Topic sentence: The most obvious reason is money.
Explanation: A car costs far more than its purchase price: fuel, insurance, tax, repairs and parking can easily add up to a fifth of an average salary, and for a vehicle that stands idle for most of the day.
Reason 2 + example: At the same time, the alternatives have improved dramatically. Metro systems, bike-sharing schemes and ride-hailing apps mean that a resident of Singapore or London can reach almost anywhere quickly without driving.
Reason 3: A third reason is environmental: many younger people are unwilling to add to the pollution and congestion that they see around them every day. (104 words)

Position: In my view, giving up the car is a good decision for most people who live in cities.
Reason 1: Financially, the savings can be invested in housing or education instead of a depreciating machine.
Reason 2: In terms of health, people who walk or cycle to public transport are naturally more active, and every car removed from a city street makes the air a little cleaner and the roads a little safer.
Acknowledging the other side (softener): Admittedly, the picture is different in rural areas, where buses may be rare and distances long, and families with small children may genuinely need a vehicle.
Answer (emphasiser): For these groups, car ownership remains practical; but they are the exception, not the rule. (110 words)

In conclusion, rising costs, better alternatives and environmental awareness explain why fewer people want a car, and for the majority who live in well-connected cities this shift is both sensible and beneficial, even if it does not suit everyone. (40 words)
About 300 words in total. Both questions answered; the opinion is clear and slightly conditional (in cities); the conclusion has closed both parts.
In conclusion, [the **points** of part 1 in one **phrase**] explain **[trend]**, and [your view in other words], **[ even if / although ]** [a small condition].
Fewer people are cooking at home and are eating ready-made or restaurant food instead. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?

Plan: Intro (trend + "this essay explains why and argues it is largely negative") → Body 1 reasons (both adults working, no time; delivery apps & ready meals convenient; cooking skills no longer passed on) → Body 2 verdict (negative: processed food → obesity/diabetes; expensive over time; shared meal lost - family time) + the other side briefly (convenience is real) → Conclusion (reasons in one phrase + negative + suggestion: cooking in the school curriculum).

**Common mistakes in combination essays:**
▸ The first question in detail, the second in one sentence.
▸ Slipping an opinion into part 1 (where only reasons are asked for).
▸ Not restating the opinion in the conclusion.
▸ Writing two separate essays - there is only one introduction and one conclusion.
Every part of the question has its own paragraph.
Narrative: no opinion unless the question asks; a suggestion at the end is fine.
Problem–solution: every solution matches a stated problem.
Combination: both parts in the introduction; both closed in the conclusion.
Every paragraph: topic sentence, explanation, example.
A neutral tone in the narrative part; a clear position in the argumentative part.

Clear position · one example · ideas at a general level · connectives correct but predictable · few mistakes, moderate range · list-sentences in places

chapters.title: Exercises (with answers) and weekly practice plan
blocks: Exercise 1 · Identify the type - A (argumentative), N (narrative), C (combination)
1. Many people believe zoos should be closed. To what extent do you agree?
2. What are the causes of childhood obesity, and what can be done to reduce it?
3. Some think university should be free; others think students should pay. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
4. More people are working from home. Why is this? Is it a positive or negative development?
5. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of international tourism.
6. Advertising aimed at children is harmful.
7. Should governments spend money on space exploration?
8. What problems does traffic congestion cause in big cities?
**Answer:** 1 A · 2 N · 3 A · 4 C · 5 N · 6 A (statement only) · 7 A (yes/no) · 8 N (problems only)
1. Although the metro is cheap, but many people prefer taxis.
2. Because the exam was hard, so most students failed.
3. Despite of the rain, the match continued.
4. Even though he studied a lot, however he did not pass.

**Answer:** 1 Although the metro is cheap, many people prefer taxis. / The metro is cheap, but … · 2 Because the exam was hard, most students failed. / The exam was hard, so … · 3 Despite the rain, … (no "of" after despite) · 4 Even though he studied a lot, he did not pass. / He studied a lot; however, he did not pass.
Words: however · for instance · as a result · moreover · in conclusion

Online shopping has grown rapidly. ___(1), it is convenient and often cheaper. ___(2), consumers can compare prices on several sites in minutes. ___(3), it has drawbacks: returns are slow and local shops lose customers. ___(4), many high streets have empty units. ___(5), online shopping is useful but has costs for communities.
**Answer:** 1 Moreover (or To begin with) · 2 For instance · 3 However · 4 As a result · 5 In conclusion
4. Prices increased ___ $500, reaching their highest level.
**Answer:** 1 by … between · 2 from … to · 3 at · 4 to
Students today face many pressures. Students must pass exams, students must find part-time work, and students also have to manage social media.
**A sample answer:** Students today face many pressures. They must pass exams and find part-time work, and young people also have to manage social media.
Exercise 6 · Find the drift - which sentence should not be in the paragraph?

(1) Public transport should be free in large cities. (2) Free buses would reduce the number of cars and therefore cut pollution. (3) They would also help poorer residents reach jobs across the city. (4) My uncle drives a bus and says the traffic gets worse every year. (5) Several European cities that have tried free transport report cleaner air and busier city centres.
**Answer:** Sentence 4 - although it is about traffic, it does not support the claim "transport should be free", and it is a personal story instead of an argument.
1. This is undoubtedly the main cause.
3. It is beyond doubt that exercise improves health.
4. Perhaps some students would prefer online classes.
5. This is the least the government can do.
**Answer:** 1 E · 2 S · 3 E · 4 S · 5 E ("least" adds emphasis here)
Exercise 8 · Write an overview (without numbers, in one sentence)
**A sample answer:** Overall, unemployment fell steadily for most of the period before rising slightly in the final years, finishing well below its starting level.
Some people think children should be taught to compete; others think they should be taught to cooperate. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
**A sample answer:** While competition can motivate a few high achievers, I believe that teaching children to cooperate produces more capable and happier adults.

Nowadays, many childrens are spending too much time on the phone. This is effect their study and their health. Parents should to limit the screen time, because it is very important for the future of the children, and also they can play outside more, and so it will be better.

**Answer:** childrens → children · This is effect → This is affecting (verb, continuous) · should to limit → should limit · the screen time → screen time · the last sentence is a run-on ("and… and… so") - break it up: …for their future. They would also play outside more, which would be better for their health. (Also "on the phone" → "on their phones")
Governments should ban all advertising aimed at children. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
Do: underline the subject matter → two columns, for/against → rank → choose a side → write the introduction (general + thesis). Then compare with the plan below.

**A sample plan:** For: children cannot judge advertising; junk-food ads drive obesity; pester power strains families. Against: ads fund children's TV; parents, not the state, should decide; a ban is hard to enforce online. Side: agree (the arguments for are strong, and the arguments against can be answered). Thesis: Although a ban may be difficult to enforce online, I firmly believe that children need this protection because they cannot recognise persuasion for what it is.
Exercise 12 · Task 1 - write an introduction + overview for this table

**A sample answer:** The table compares the percentage of commuters using five forms of transport in one city in 2000 and 2020. Overall, the car remained the most common choice in both years but lost a substantial share, while rail and cycling grew markedly and walking was unchanged.

One Task 1 (line/bar) in 20 minutes; check it against the Chapter 2 checklist
Only plan three Task 2 questions (type, two columns, thesis) - no writing
One Task 2 in 40 minutes; mark it yourself with the Chapter 1 self-test
Rewrite Tuesday's essay after reading the AI feedback; compare with a Band 7 sample
Review your error log; 10 topic words; rest

**How to keep an error log:** three columns on one page - mistake · correction · how many times. After each piece of writing, add new mistakes. In the last 5 minutes of the exam, look only for the three that come up most often. Within a month, most students' top-3 mistakes change - meaning the earlier ones have been cured.

This is the end of the book. Print the checklist from every chapter together and keep it in front of you; after every practice, mark yourself with it. In Writing, your band rises through habit, not magic.
